course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 2
unit.description: Follow the Spanish, French, Dutch, and British colonies, the regions of British North America, Atlantic trade, slavery, and colonial society from 1607 to 1754.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Slavery in the British Colonies
lesson.summary: How slavery spread through the British colonies, how colonial laws created a racial system of chattel slavery, and how enslaved Africans resisted and preserved their culture.
learningGoals: Explain why British colonies participated in the Atlantic slave trade and how participation differed by region.
Explain how slave codes created a racial system of hereditary, lifelong slavery.
Explain how enslaved people resisted slavery and maintained family, culture, and religion.
lesson.bigIdea: Slavery grew because land was abundant and labor was scarce, colonial laws made it hereditary and racial, and enslaved people resisted it openly and in everyday ways while preserving their own culture.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain the causes and effects of slavery in the British colonial regions and how enslaved people responded. Keep each region's economy in mind.

sections.title: The slave trade and the colonies
sections.conceptTitle: The slave trade and the colonies

blocks.text: All the British colonies took part to varying degrees in the Atlantic slave trade. The reasons were an abundance of land, a growing European demand for colonial goods, and a shortage of indentured servants. Enslaved Africans endured the Middle Passage, the forced voyage across the Atlantic, in crowded and unhealthy ships, and many died on the way.

The extent of slavery depended on the economy. Small New England farms used relatively few enslaved laborers, and all port cities held significant minorities of enslaved people. The emerging plantation systems of the Chesapeake and the southern Atlantic coast had large numbers of enslaved workers. The great majority of enslaved Africans, however, were sent to the West Indies.

sections.takeaway: Land, demand for colonial goods, and a shortage of servants drew all British colonies into the slave trade, with plantation regions using the most enslaved labor.

sections.title: Chattel slavery and the law

blocks.text: In the early 1600s the legal status of Africans in Virginia was unsettled, and some became free. As chattel slavery, in which people are legal property and slavery is lifelong, became the dominant labor system in many southern colonies, new laws created a strict racial system. Slave codes restricted where enslaved people could go and what they could do, and they prohibited interracial relationships. A Virginia law of 1662 defined the children of enslaved mothers as enslaved, so slavery passed from mother to child. In this way the descendants of African American mothers were defined as black and enslaved in perpetuity.

Many historians argue that planters' fear of unrest also pushed them toward slavery. In Bacon's Rebellion in 1676, poor white and Black laborers in Virginia joined an armed revolt against the colonial elite, and afterward planters relied more heavily on African slavery, which also let them use race to divide laborers.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Slavery was not simply a leftover of earlier labor systems. Colonial legislatures wrote laws that made it racial, hereditary, and permanent.

sections.takeaway: Colonial laws made slavery a racial, hereditary, lifelong status.

sections.title: Resistance and culture

blocks.text: Africans developed both overt and covert means to resist the dehumanizing nature of slavery. Overt resistance included armed revolt. In 1739, in the Stono Rebellion in South Carolina, a group of enslaved people seized weapons, killed several colonists, and marched toward Spanish Florida before militia defeated them. South Carolina responded with a harsher slave code. Others fled to Spanish Florida, where Spain offered freedom to those who converted to Catholicism.

Covert resistance included working slowly, damaging tools, feigning illness, and learning in secret. Enslaved people also maintained their family and gender systems, culture, and religion. African languages, music, foods, and names blended with new influences, as in the Gullah culture of the South Carolina coast, and enslaved people formed their own religious communities.

sections.takeaway: Enslaved people resisted through revolt, flight, and daily acts of defiance and kept their families, cultures, and religions alive.

connections.title: Slavery and colonial society
connections.body: Slavery shaped the economy and law of the colonies. Topic 2.7 looks at the wider colonial society and how ideas and religion crossed the Atlantic.
connections.transferQuestion: How did colonial law turn a labor system into a racial system?
connections.feedback: A strong answer names a specific rule, such as hereditary status through the mother or bans on interracial relationships, and explains how it fixed race and slavery together.
